extracted.intended_audience: poets and aspiring verse-writers (especially satirists and those considering epic)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, Horatian advice for composing and revising verse—choosing appropriate genre, shaping material for a fitting audience, avoiding reckless invective, and cultivating craft and discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid slavish imitation of Greek models
rubrics_metrics.description: “Seek you the throng of Grecian bards to swell? Take sticks into a forest just as well.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not blindly ape Greek poets or transplant foreign mannerisms that do not suit you; imitation for its own sake is futile and misses what is native and appropriate to your own voice and circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a form and subject suited to your abilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace admits: “Would that I could... but skill and vigour lack... Not every one can paint in epic strain ... For me, this walk of satire ... Best suits my gait.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the genre (satire, epic, pastoral, stage) that matches your talents and temperament rather than forcing yourself into a form you cannot sustain; recognise the technical and rhetorical demands of each form before attempting it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise persistently; polish your work
rubrics_metrics.description: “Oh yes! believe me, you must draw your pen Not once nor twice but o'er and o'er again ... He'd prune redundancies, apply the file To each excrescence that deforms his style.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revision is essential: repeatedly edit and cut redundancies until the piece entices a reader to return; polishing matters more than immediate popular applause. Example/anti-pattern: leaving raw first drafts as final work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for a fitting, discerning audience rather than the mob
rubrics_metrics.description: “Not making popular applause your cue, But looking to fit audience, although few.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to please informed, judicious readers (friends, patrons, fellow poets) rather than pandering to fickle crowds or the hooting masses; cultivate critics whose commendation is meaningful (Maecenas, Virgil, Varius are named as desirable readers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious in lampoon and invective; avoid needlessly attacking the powerful
rubrics_metrics.description: Lines and images: “This poor implement of mine, my pen, Shall ne'er assault one soul of living men: Like a sheathed sword, I'll carry it about ... If a man writes ill verses out of spite 'Gainst A or B, the sufferer may indict.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustain moral/practical prudence: sharp lampoon risks retaliation or legal action. Prefer measured satire and avoid recklessly naming or persecuting powerful figures—the poet may protect himself by restraint and judgment about targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make sense and scan: prioritize clarity and metrical craft
rubrics_metrics.description: “He, anxious only to make sense and scan, Pours forth two hundred verses ... To drill reluctant words into a line, This was Lucilius' hobby, and 'tis mine.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for both sense (clarity of thought) and correct verse-metre; drill and wrestle with lines until both meaning and rhythm cohere. Hasty production that sacrifices sense or scansion is an inferior practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain discipline; write regularly and resist sloth
rubrics_metrics.description: Damasippus reproves: “So seldom do you write... You blame your pens... stop your ears to sloth's enchanting voice, Or give up your best hopes: there lies your choice.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid procrastination and intermittent bursts; cultivate steady practice and industry. Sloth prevents the production of worthwhile material; persistent effort is required to fulfil poetic ambitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation and blind imitation of social superiors
rubrics_metrics.description: Damasippus: “You build, which means you try To ape great men... if Maecenas does a thing, must you, His weaker every way, attempt it too?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mimic the styles, tastes, or public gestures of patrons or famous contemporaries as a way to claim stature; cultivate an authentic voice rather than affectations borrowed from those above you.
